VisRetain: how the model sees your image

Qwen2.5-VL-3B, running on this machine. Each stage shows what the model does, the math with your image's own numbers, and the check that proves it.

1 · Image → tokens2 · Attention3 · RoundingFull pipeline
Stage 1 · Image → visual tokens
How Qwen cuts your image into the pieces it remembers, and the proof that we know exactly which piece is which.

Every later stage of VisRetain colours these squares (which ones the model keeps, which it throws away). So before anything else we need to know, for certain, which square of your image each stored token stands for.

1

Your image

2

Resize to a grid of px squares

Qwen needs both sides to be a whole number of squares, and keeps the total within a pixel budget.

3

Cut into × px patches

Each patch becomes one row of numbers in the model's input. Hover over the image to inspect a patch.

4

Merge each 2 × 2 block of patches into one token

The language model stores one token per × px square. These are the tokens VisRetain tracks. Hover to see a token's number, row, column and position.

5

The vision encoder turns patches into tokens

6

The tokens join the prompt

What the language model actually reads: the chat template, the image as one block of tokens, then your question. Each image token gets a 3D position (time, row, column).

7

Proof: change one square, see which token reacts

Steps 3–6 come from reading Qwen's code. To prove the model really behaves that way, we invert the colours of one square and run the real vision encoder twice. Left: with the encoder's mixing switched off (each token can only look at itself), exactly one token should change, the one we predicted. That tests the mapping with nothing to hide behind. Right: the encoder as it really runs, where tokens look at their neighbours, so the change spreads. Red = how much each token's output changed. Click any square to test it yourself.
